name: Join nodes & renew certificates
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Drill EVERY node-level kubeadm corner harder than the exam: inspect component versions, read the kubelet config and static-pod manifests, mint a worker join token, perform the drain/uncordon maintenance dance, renew control-plane certificates, read an upgrade plan, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. All graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state.

questions.title: Generate a worker join command
questions.teach:
To add a worker, mint a fresh bootstrap token and print the full join line in one shot: `kubeadm token create --print-join-command`. This creates a Secret named `bootstrap-token-<id>` of type `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token` in `kube-system`.

**Gotcha:** find these Secrets by TYPE, not name — `kubectl -n kube-system get secrets --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`.
questions.prompt:
On $CP, generate a fresh worker join command with kubeadm so a NEW bootstrap-token Secret is created in `kube-system`.

Target: strictly MORE bootstrap-token Secrets exist in `kube-system` than when the step started.
questions.hint: `docker exec "$CP" kubeadm token create --print-join-command`. Verify with `kubectl -n kube-system get secrets --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" kubeadm token create --print-join-command
kubectl -n kube-system get secrets --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token

verification.description: a NEW bootstrap-token Secret was created in kube-system (count increased)

questions.eli5:
Imagine your cluster is a members-only club, and you want to let a new worker machine in the door. The bouncer won't let just anyone join — the newcomer needs a **one-time guest pass** plus a way to confirm the club is really the club (and not an imposter).

A kubeadm **bootstrap token** is that guest pass. The single command:

```
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
```

does two friendly things at once: it mints a brand-new token, and it prints the *entire* `kubeadm join ...` line — IP, token, and a certificate fingerprint (the "is this really the club?" check) — so you can copy-paste it on the new worker.

Behind the scenes, that token is stored as a **Secret** in the `kube-system` area. But here's the twist: it's named `bootstrap-token-<random id>`, not something obvious. So if you go looking for it by name, you'll miss it. You find it by its **type** instead: `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Don't search by name — search by type.** `kubectl -n kube-system get secrets --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`.
- Tokens **expire** (24 hours by default). An expired token means the worker can't join — mint a fresh one.
- The token is a **credential**. Anyone holding it can join a node to your cluster, so treat it like a password.
- `--print-join-command` just prints; it doesn't join anything itself. You still run the printed line *on the worker*.
- The default token is throwaway. For permanent setups you'd set a TTL or delete it after use.
questions.deepDive:
## Bootstrap tokens & worker join — full rundown

### Mental model
A new node joins a kubeadm cluster by presenting a short-lived **bootstrap token** to the API server. The token lets the node (a) authenticate just enough to request a real kubelet client certificate (TLS bootstrap), and (b) be trusted via a CA fingerprint so it isn't tricked by a fake control plane. Each token is stored as a **Secret of type `bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token`** in `kube-system`.

### Minting a token and the join command
```bash
# create a token AND print the full join line in one shot
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
# -> kubeadm join 172.18.0.2:6443 --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef \
#       --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hex>

# just create a token (prints the token id.secret)
kubeadm token create

# create with a custom lifetime
kubeadm token create --ttl 1h
kubeadm token create --ttl 0          # 0 = never expires (avoid in prod)

# list / delete tokens
kubeadm token list
kubeadm token delete <token-id>       # <id> is the part before the dot
```

The printed `kubeadm join` line is run **on the worker**, not the control plane.

### Anatomy of a token
A token looks like `abcdef.0123456789abcdef`:
| Part | Length | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Token ID | 6 chars `[a-z0-9]` | public identifier; becomes `bootstrap-token-<id>` Secret name |
| Token Secret | 16 chars `[a-z0-9]` | the private half |

### The join command's three parts
| Flag | What it is | How to recompute if lost |
|---|---|---|
| `<apiserver>:6443` | control-plane endpoint | `kubectl cluster-info` |
| `--token` | the bootstrap token | `kubeadm token create` |
| `--discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:…` | hash of the cluster CA public key (anti-MITM) | see below |

Recompute the CA cert hash:
```bash
openssl x509 -pubkey -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt \
 | openssl rsa -pubin -outform der 2>/dev/null \
 | openssl dgst -sha256 -hex | sed 's/^.* //'
```

### Finding the token Secrets (by TYPE, not name)
The Secret is named `bootstrap-token-<id>`, so filter by type:
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get secrets \
  --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token
```
```yaml
# a bootstrap-token Secret (data base64-decoded for readability)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
type: bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token
metadata:
  name: bootstrap-token-abcdef
  namespace: kube-system
stringData:
  token-id: abcdef
  token-secret: 0123456789abcdef
  expiration: "2026-11-02T10:00:00Z"
  usage-bootstrap-authentication: "true"
  usage-bootstrap-signing: "true"
  auth-extra-groups: system:bootstrappers:kubeadm:default-node-token
```

### Token lifetime & defaults
| Property | Default |
|---|---|
| TTL | **24h** (`--ttl 24h0m0s`) |
| `--ttl 0` | never expires |
| Usages | `signing`, `authentication` |
| Group granted | `system:bootstrappers:kubeadm:default-node-token` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Find by type, not name** — the random `bootstrap-token-<id>` name is unpredictable.
- Tokens **expire after 24h** by default; an expired token fails the join — create a fresh one.
- `--print-join-command` prints only; the actual join runs on the worker node.
- For a **second control-plane** node you also need `--control-plane --certificate-key <key>`; upload certs first with `kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs` (that cert key expires in 2h).
- Treat the join command as a secret — it grants cluster membership.
- `kubeadm token create` (no `--ttl`) uses the 24h default; use `kubeadm token list` to see expiry.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubeadm token create --print-join-command        # mint + full join line
kubectl -n kube-system get secrets \
  --field-selector type=bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token   # verify new Secret
kubeadm token list                                # see all tokens + expiry
```

questions.title: Renew control-plane certificates
questions.teach:
kubeadm control-plane certs under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/` last ONE year. Check them with `kubeadm certs check-expiration`, then renew with `kubeadm certs renew apiserver` (or `renew all`), pushing NotAfter ~1 year out and writing a fresh cert (new serial).

**Gotcha:** renewal rewrites the cert on disk but does NOT restart the static pod — the running apiserver keeps the old cert until its manifest is bounced.
questions.prompt:
On $CP, check cert expiration, then renew the apiserver certificate so a fresh cert (new serial, NotAfter ~1 year out) is written.

Target: `/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt` on $CP has a DIFFERENT serial than when the step started, and its NotAfter is >300 days out.
questions.hint: `docker exec "$CP" kubeadm certs check-expiration`, then `docker exec "$CP" kubeadm certs renew apiserver`. Confirm: `docker exec "$CP" openssl x509 -enddate -serial -noout -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt`.
questions.solution:
docker exec "$CP" kubeadm certs check-expiration
docker exec "$CP" kubeadm certs renew apiserver
docker exec "$CP" openssl x509 -enddate -serial -noout -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt

verification.description: apiserver.crt serial changed AND NotAfter is >300 days out (renewed)

questions.eli5:
Think of your cluster's certificates like the ID badges that let the control-plane components prove who they are to each other. kubeadm issues these badges when it builds the cluster, and — like a real passport — each one has an **expiry date, exactly one year out**. If a badge expires, the component can't prove its identity anymore and things start failing (the API server stops trusting connections).

So there are two moves here:

1. **Check the expiry dates** — `kubeadm certs check-expiration`. This is like laying all your passports on the table and reading the "valid until" date on each.
2. **Renew one (or all)** — `kubeadm certs renew apiserver` (or `renew all`). This prints a fresh badge with a new photo (a new serial number) and pushes the expiry date back another year.

The sneaky part: renewing only swaps the badge *on the shelf* (the file on disk). The component that's already running is still wearing the **old** badge. It won't pick up the new one until you make it restart.

**Watch out for:**

- **Renewal writes the new cert to disk but does NOT restart the component.** The running API server keeps using the old cert until its static-pod manifest is bounced (e.g. briefly move `kube-apiserver.yaml` out of `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` and back, or restart the kubelet).
- A renewed cert has a **new serial number** and a NotAfter ~365 days out — that's how you confirm it actually renewed.
- `kubeadm upgrade apply` **auto-renews** all certs as a side effect — that's why clusters upgraded yearly rarely hit expiry.
- The cluster **CA** itself lasts ~10 years; you're renewing the *leaf* certs it signs, not the CA.
- `kubelet.conf` client cert usually **auto-rotates**; the ones you renew by hand are the control-plane certs under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/`.
questions.deepDive:
## Renewing control-plane certificates — full rundown

### Mental model
kubeadm runs its own PKI. A long-lived **CA** (`/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt`, ~10 years) signs many short-lived **leaf certificates** (apiserver, etcd, kubelet-client, front-proxy, etc.), each valid for **1 year**. If a leaf expires, that component can no longer authenticate — the API server rejects connections and the cluster effectively breaks. You renew leaves with `kubeadm certs renew`; the CA is not touched.

### Where the certs live
```
/etc/kubernetes/pki/
├── ca.crt / ca.key                     # cluster CA (~10y)
├── apiserver.crt / apiserver.key       # API server serving cert
├── apiserver-kubelet-client.crt/.key   # apiserver -> kubelet
├── apiserver-etcd-client.crt/.key
├── front-proxy-ca.crt / front-proxy-client.crt
└── etcd/
    ├── ca.crt / ca.key                 # etcd CA
    ├── server.crt / peer.crt / healthcheck-client.crt
```
Kubeconfig-embedded certs: `/etc/kubernetes/{admin,controller-manager,scheduler}.conf`.

### Check expiration
```bash
kubeadm certs check-expiration
```
```
CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME   EXTERNALLY MANAGED
admin.conf                 Nov 01, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d            no
apiserver                  Nov 01, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d            no
apiserver-etcd-client      Nov 01, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d            no
...
CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY      EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME
ca                         Oct 30, 2035 10:00 UTC   9y
```

### Renew
```bash
kubeadm certs renew apiserver        # one cert
kubeadm certs renew all              # every kubeadm-managed leaf + kubeconfigs
```
| Command | Renews |
|---|---|
| `kubeadm certs renew apiserver` | the apiserver serving cert only |
| `kubeadm certs renew all` | all leaf certs + `admin/controller-manager/scheduler.conf` |
| `kubeadm certs renew <name>` | a single named cert (see `check-expiration` names) |

Renewal rewrites the `.crt` (and uses the existing CA to re-sign), giving a **new serial** and a **NotAfter ~1 year out**.

### Confirm it renewed
```bash
openssl x509 -enddate -serial -noout -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
# notAfter=Nov  1 10:00:00 2027 GMT
# serial=1A2B3C...        <- changed vs before
```

### The critical catch: renewal ≠ restart
`kubeadm certs renew` only updates files on disk. The **running** component (a static Pod) keeps the old cert in memory until its Pod restarts:
```bash
# force the apiserver static Pod to reload (any of these):
mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/ && sleep 20 \
  && mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# or
crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver        # find and kill the container
# or
systemctl restart kubelet              # kubelet re-reconciles all static Pods
```

### Automatic renewal
- **`kubeadm upgrade apply`** renews all certs as a side effect (disable with `--certificate-renewal=false`). This is why yearly-upgraded clusters rarely expire.
- The **kubelet client cert** (`/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem`) auto-rotates when `rotateCertificates: true`.
- `admin.conf` does **not** auto-rotate — renew it manually or via upgrade.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Renew writes the file but does not restart the component** — you must bounce the static Pod (or kubelet) for the new cert to take effect.
- A successful renewal shows a **new serial** and **NotAfter ~365 days out** — grade on both.
- You renew **leaf** certs; the **CA** (~10y) is separate and renewing it is a much bigger operation.
- Certs live on the **node** under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/`, read with `openssl`, not `kubectl`.
- `check-expiration` also flags `EXTERNALLY MANAGED` certs — kubeadm won't renew those.
- Clock skew on the node makes expiry math wrong — ensure NTP is correct.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubeadm certs check-expiration                              # read dates
kubeadm certs renew apiserver                               # (or: renew all)
openssl x509 -enddate -serial -noout -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
# then restart the static Pod so it picks up the new cert
```
